status: Exact and rigorous results exist for selected stochastic or special models. Generic deterministic systems remain difficult, especially in low dimensions.
why: Derives a basic macroscopic transport law from microscopic mechanics.
key_works: Bonetto, Lebowitz, and Rey-Bellet, 2000, *Fourier’s Law: A Challenge to Theorists*, math-ph/0002052.

title: Exact structure of 2+1-dimensional KPZ universality
subfield: Statistical mechanics and nonequilibrium quantum matter
open: Determine exact critical exponents, distributions, or an equivalent solvable characterization of the strong-coupling Kardar–Parisi–Zhang universality class in two spatial dimensions.
status: One-dimensional KPZ is far more analytically developed. Higher-dimensional exponents are primarily numerical.
why: Explains broad classes of nonequilibrium growth and fluctuating interfaces.
key_works: Kardar, Parisi, and Zhang, 1986, *Dynamic Scaling of Growing Interfaces*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.889; Halpin-Healy and Takeuchi, 2015, *A KPZ Cocktail—Shaken, Not Stirred…*, arXiv:1505.01910.

title: Entropy production from partially observed trajectories
subfield: Statistical mechanics and nonequilibrium quantum matter
open: Infer tight, experimentally useful bounds on total entropy production when only a subset of variables is observed and dynamics may be non-Markovian.
status: Fluctuation theorems and thermodynamic uncertainty relations solve important idealized cases; hidden dissipation remains difficult to reconstruct.
why: Makes nonequilibrium thermodynamics operational in cells and nanoscale devices.
key_works: Udo Seifert, 2012, *Stochastic Thermodynamics, Fluctuation Theorems, and Molecular Machines*, arXiv:1205.4176.

title: Universal description of frictional jamming
subfield: Soft matter, granular matter, and active materials
open: Predict jamming thresholds and mechanical response as functions of friction, particle shape, preparation history, and contact-network evolution.
status: Frictionless spherical-particle jamming is much better organized theoretically than realistic frictional grains.
why: Supports reliable modeling of powders, soils, and dense suspensions.
key_works: Liu and Nagel, 2010, *The Jamming Transition and the Marginally Jammed Solid*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-conmatphys-070909-104045.

title: Yielding universality in amorphous solids
subfield: Soft matter, granular matter, and active materials
open: Determine which yielding transitions share universal critical behavior and which depend on preparation, aging, temperature, or interaction range.
status: Elastoplastic models and simulations reveal avalanche scaling, but brittle yielding, ductile flow, and finite-temperature behavior are not unified.
why: Predicts failure and flow in glasses, pastes, and amorphous materials.
key_works: Bonn et al., 2017, *Yield Stress Materials in Soft Condensed Matter*, arXiv:1502.05281; DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.89.035005.

title: Predictive discontinuous shear thickening
subfield: Soft matter, granular matter, and active materials
open: Predict when a real suspension abruptly thickens, including contact activation, particle roughness, boundary effects, and transient loading.
status: Frictional-contact models explain much of the phenomenon; quantitative transfer across particle chemistries and industrial formulations remains incomplete.
why: Enables better processing and impact-responsive materials.
key_works: Wyart and Cates, 2014, *Discontinuous Shear Thickening without Inertia in Dense Non-Brownian Suspensions*, arXiv:1311.4099.

title: Gardner phase in finite-dimensional structural glasses
subfield: Soft matter, granular matter, and active materials
open: Determine whether a sharp Gardner transition survives in realistic finite-dimensional glasses or becomes an avoided transition or crossover.
status: Mean-field theory predicts hierarchical marginal states; simulations and experiments give suggestive but interpretation-dependent signatures.
why: Links glass stability, marginality, and mechanical response.
key_works: Charbonneau et al., 2014, *Fractal Free Energy Landscapes in Structural Glasses*; Berthier et al., 2019, *Gardner Physics in Amorphous Solids and Beyond*.

title: Motility-induced phase separation with realistic interactions
subfield: Soft matter, granular matter, and active materials
open: Establish when motility-induced phase separation survives hydrodynamics, alignment, inertia, chemical signaling, and particle asymmetry in experimentally realistic active suspensions.
status: Minimal models exhibit clear phase separation; adding real-world interactions can qualitatively alter it.
why: Turns an idealized active-matter mechanism into a predictive material principle.
key_works: Cates and Tailleur, 2015, *Motility-Induced Phase Separation*, arXiv:1406.3533.

title: Statistical theory of active turbulence
subfield: Soft matter, granular matter, and active materials
open: Derive predictive statistics for defect creation, annihilation, flow spectra, and energy transfer in active turbulent phases across geometry and activity.
status: Continuum theories reproduce characteristic chaotic flows, but universal scaling and defect–flow closures remain incomplete.
why: Enables control of self-driven materials and biological flows.
key_works: Marchetti et al., 2013, *Hydrodynamics of Soft Active Matter*, arXiv:1207.2929.

title: Predictive moving-contact-line law
subfield: Soft matter, granular matter, and active materials
open: Derive a transferable law for contact-line motion on realistic heterogeneous surfaces, connecting molecular slip, hysteresis, evaporation, and macroscopic fluid motion.
status: The classical no-slip singularity is understood; many regularizations exist, but choosing and parameterizing them predictively remains difficult.
why: Improves coating, printing, condensation, and microfluidics.
key_works: Huh and Scriven, 1971, *Hydrodynamic Model of Steady Movement of a Solid/Liquid/Fluid Contact Line*; Snoeijer and Andreotti, 2013, *Moving Contact Lines: Scales, Regimes, and Dynamical Transitions*.

title: Polymer entanglement under strong deformation
subfield: Soft matter, granular matter, and active materials
open: Predict stress, disentanglement, and recovery of real polymer melts under strong, complex flows from molecular architecture without extensive empirical closure.
status: Tube and reptation models capture many regimes; branching, constraint release, nonlinear flow, and failure require additional modeling.
why: Enables predictable manufacturing and recycling of polymeric materials.
key_works: de Gennes, 1971, *Reptation of a Polymer Chain in the Presence of Fixed Obstacles*; Doi and Edwards, 1986, *The Theory of Polymer Dynamics*.

title: Three-dimensional Navier–Stokes regularity
open: Prove global smoothness or construct finite-time breakdown for the incompressible three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations under the Clay problem’s conditions.
status: Global weak solutions have been known since Leray; smoothness and uniqueness in the required generality remain open.
why: Resolves a foundational question about deterministic fluid evolution.
key_works: Jean Leray, 1934, *Sur le Mouvement d’un Liquide Visqueux Emplissant l’Espace*; Charles Fefferman, 2000, *Existence and Smoothness of the Navier–Stokes Equation*.
prize: US$1 million Clay Millennium Prize, subject to its rules.

title: Turbulent intermittency exponents
open: Derive anomalous scaling exponents and extreme-event statistics of three-dimensional turbulence from the governing equations rather than empirical multifractal fits.
status: Kolmogorov’s 1941 theory gives a baseline; intermittency corrections remain incompletely understood.
why: Predicts rare, intense events important for mixing, loads, and reaction rates.
key_works: Uriel Frisch, 1995, *Turbulence: The Legacy of A. N. Kolmogorov*, DOI: 10.1017/CBO9781139170666.

title: Asymptotic wall-turbulence law
open: Determine the correct high-Reynolds-number scaling of wall turbulence, including logarithmic-law coefficients, outer-layer interactions, and universality limits.
status: Experiments and simulations span growing ranges but remain far from many engineering and geophysical regimes.
why: Improves drag and heat-transfer prediction at realistic scales.
key_works: Marusic et al., 2010, *Wall-Bounded Turbulent Flows at High Reynolds Numbers: Recent Advances and Key Issues*; Smits, McKeon, and Marusic, 2011, *High-Reynolds Number Wall Turbulence*.

title: Three-dimensional turbulent separation prediction
open: Predict separation onset, reattachment, and unsteady loads in three-dimensional turbulent boundary layers without geometry-specific tuning.
status: Reynolds-averaged models remain unreliable in many strongly separated flows; high-fidelity simulation is often too expensive.
why: Reduces design uncertainty in vehicles, turbines, and aerodynamic systems.
key_works: Simpson, 1989, *Turbulent Boundary-Layer Separation*; Spalart, 2009, *Detached-Eddy Simulation*.

title: Turbulent entrainment closure
open: Predict entrainment rates across turbulent/non-turbulent interfaces for jets, plumes, wakes, and stratified flows from local physics and large-scale constraints.
status: Empirical entrainment coefficients work within classes but vary with buoyancy, geometry, and intermittency.
why: Improves models of pollution, fires, clouds, and industrial mixing.
key_works: da Silva et al., 2014, *Interfacial Layers between Regions of Different Turbulence Intensity*; Frisch, 1995, *Turbulence*.

title: Roughness-to-drag prediction
open: Predict drag and heat transfer from measured three-dimensional surface topography across roughness shapes and Reynolds numbers without dedicated calibration for each surface.
status: Equivalent-sand-grain descriptions compress observations but do not uniquely follow from arbitrary topography.
why: Enables rational design and maintenance of ships, pipes, and turbines.
key_works: Flack and Schultz, 2010, *Review of Hydraulic Roughness Scales in the Fully Rough Regime*; Jiménez, 2004, *Turbulent Flows over Rough Walls*.

title: Net-positive large-scale active drag reduction
open: Demonstrate sustained drag reduction whose saved power substantially exceeds actuation, sensing, and control costs under realistic fouling and changing flow conditions.
status: Large drag reductions occur in selected laboratory conditions; net energy benefit and robustness often diminish during scale-up.
why: Reduces transportation and pumping energy.
key_works: Quadrio, 2011, *Drag Reduction in Turbulent Boundary Layers by In-Plane Wall Motion*; Choi, Jeon, and Kim, 2008, *Control of Flow over a Bluff Body*.

title: Classical-to-quantum turbulent cascade crossover
open: Determine how energy passes from large-scale superfluid flow through vortex dynamics to Kelvin waves and dissipative excitations, with quantitatively testable spectra.
status: Different temperature regimes and vortex configurations support competing crossover pictures.
why: Connects turbulence to quantized topological defects.
key_works: Barenghi, Skrbek, and Sreenivasan, 2014, *Introduction to Quantum Turbulence*, arXiv:1404.1909.

title: Net-electric fusion power
open: Operate a fusion system that exports sustained net electricity after accounting for drivers, magnets, cryogenics, fuel processing, cooling, and maintenance.
status: Plasma gain and target gain are not net-electric gain. Integrated electricity production remains a stronger engineering target.
why: Establishes fusion as an energy technology rather than only a plasma milestone.
key_works: National Academies, 2021, *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI: 10.17226/25991.

title: Closed tritium fuel cycle
open: Demonstrate an integrated deuterium–tritium fuel cycle with adequate breeding margin, extraction, inventory control, processing speed, and startup supply.
status: Component tests and blanket designs exist; neutron economy alone does not establish plant-level self-sufficiency.
why: Determines whether deuterium–tritium fusion can expand beyond limited external fuel supplies.
key_works: National Academies, 2021, *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*.

title: Disruption avoidance at reactor conditions
open: Predict and avoid damaging plasma disruptions across operating scenarios with sufficiently low missed-event and false-alarm rates, and validated fallback mitigation.
status: Machine-learning predictors and mitigation experiments improve performance but must generalize across machines and operating regimes.
why: Protects reactor structures and supports high availability.
key_works: Hender et al., 2007, *Chapter 3: MHD Stability, Operational Limits and Disruptions*; de Vries et al., 2011, *Survey of Disruption Causes at JET*.

title: Reactor-compatible divertor exhaust
open: Exhaust reactor-level heat and particles while preserving core confinement, controlling impurities, and keeping target erosion and component temperatures acceptable.
status: Detached plasmas and advanced geometries offer partial solutions; integrated compatibility remains the key constraint.
why: Prevents plasma-facing components from becoming the limiting reactor subsystem.
key_works: Leonard, 2018, *Plasma Detachment in Divertor Tokamaks*; National Academies, 2021, *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*.

title: Fusion-neutron material lifetime
open: Demonstrate structural and functional materials with acceptable toughness, dimensional stability, activation, and property retention under relevant fusion-neutron spectra and accumulated damage.
status: Fission irradiation and ion beams provide partial surrogates; helium production and coupled damage complicate extrapolation.
why: Determines replacement schedules, waste characteristics, and plant economics.
key_works: Zinkle and Ghoniem, 2000, *Operating Temperature Windows for Fusion Reactor Structural Materials*; Zinkle and Snead, 2014, *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*.

title: Repetitive, efficient inertial-fusion driver and target system
open: Integrate sufficiently efficient drivers, inexpensive targets, high repetition rate, accurate injection, and chamber clearing into a sustained inertial-fusion energy system.
status: Ignition experiments demonstrate target physics; they do not by themselves establish repetitive economic operation.
why: Converts individual high-gain shots into a possible power plant.
key_works: National Research Council, 2013, *An Assessment of the Prospects for Inertial Fusion Energy*; National Academies, 2021, *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*.

title: Reconnection energy partition
open: Predict how three-dimensional magnetic reconnection divides released energy among bulk flow, electron heating, ion heating, and nonthermal particles across plasma regimes.
status: Kinetic simulations and spacecraft observations establish multiple mechanisms; a transferable closure remains incomplete.
why: Connects magnetic topology changes to observable heating and acceleration.
key_works: Zweibel and Yamada, 2009, *Magnetic Reconnection in Astrophysical and Laboratory Plasmas*; Califano et al., 2020, *Electron-Only Reconnection in Plasma Turbulence*, DOI: 10.3389/fphy.2020.00317.

title: Predictive low-temperature plasma chemistry
open: Predict species concentrations, surface reactions, and energy efficiency in technologically relevant nonequilibrium plasmas using validated cross sections and reaction networks.
status: Models often depend on incomplete rate data and poorly known surface conditions; transfer between reactors is limited.
why: Improves semiconductor processing, chemical conversion, and plasma-enabled treatment.
key_works: Adamovich et al., 2022, *The 2022 Plasma Roadmap: Low Temperature Plasma Science and Technology*, DOI: 10.1088/1361-6463/ac5e1c.

title: Vacuum Schwinger pair production
open: Observe electron–positron creation from the vacuum by an applied electromagnetic field in a regime that cleanly identifies the nonperturbative Schwinger mechanism.
status: Predicted in 1951. Strong-field pair production through other mechanisms is not the same observation.
why: Tests a central nonperturbative prediction of quantum electrodynamics.
key_works: Julian Schwinger, 1951, *On Gauge Invariance and Vacuum Polarization*; Di Piazza et al., 2012, *Extremely High-Intensity Laser Interactions with Fundamental Quantum Systems*, arXiv:1111.3886.

title: Laboratory optical vacuum birefringence
open: Measure the polarization-dependent refractive response of the quantum vacuum to a controlled applied field, excluding material and instrumental birefringence.
status: Strong theoretical prediction and astrophysical indications do not replace a clean laboratory optical measurement.
why: Directly tests nonlinear vacuum electrodynamics.
key_works: Heisenberg and Euler, 1936, *Folgerungen aus der Diracschen Theorie des Positrons*; Di Piazza et al., 2012, arXiv:1111.3886.

title: Nonperturbative strong-field QED regime
open: Reach and diagnose regimes where higher-order strong-field quantum corrections qualitatively alter predictions, with controlled beam and field characterization.
status: Existing experiments constrain radiation reaction and strong-field processes; accessing the most extreme quantum regime remains a distinct target.
why: Tests the breakdown of commonly used perturbative descriptions.
key_works: Yakimenko et al., 2019, *Prospect of Studying Nonperturbative QED with Beam–Beam Collisions*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.122.190404.

title: Quantum-coherent microwave–optical transduction
open: Convert quantum states between microwave and optical frequencies with simultaneously high efficiency, low added noise, adequate bandwidth, and compatible cryogenic operation.
status: Multiple physical platforms demonstrate conversion; optimizing one metric often worsens another.
why: Connects superconducting quantum processors to optical networks.
key_works: Lauk et al., 2020, *Perspectives on Quantum Transduction*; Han et al., 2021, *Microwave–Optical Quantum Frequency Conversion*; Caleffi et al., 2025, *Quantum Transduction: Enabling Quantum Networking*, arXiv:2505.02057.

title: Deterministic low-loss photonic entangling gate
open: Implement a scalable two-photon entangling gate with sufficiently low loss and error for fault tolerance, including sources, mode matching, and feed-forward.
status: Linear-optical and matter-mediated approaches achieve important demonstrations, but deterministic high-performance integration remains difficult.
why: Enables practical photonic quantum computation and networking.
key_works: Knill, Laflamme, and Milburn, 2001, *A Scheme for Efficient Quantum Computation with Linear Optics*; Shapiro, 2006, *Single-Photon Kerr Nonlinearities Do Not Help Quantum Computation*.

title: Broadband, efficient, manufacturable metalenses
open: Achieve a specified combination of aperture, numerical aperture, bandwidth, polarization tolerance, efficiency, and fabrication yield while approaching known dispersion limits.
status: Impressive devices exist, but broad-bandwidth and large-aperture performance face fundamental and manufacturing tradeoffs.
why: Enables compact optical systems without hiding losses or bandwidth restrictions.
key_works: Quevedo-Teruel et al., 2019, *Roadmap on Metasurfaces*, DOI: 10.1088/2040-8986/ab161d; Presutti and Monticone, 2020, *Focusing on Bandwidth: Achromatic Metalens Limits*.

title: Thermal Casimir-force material-response puzzle
open: Reconcile precision force measurements with a physically consistent treatment of low-frequency electromagnetic response and thermal fluctuations.
status: Predictions using different metallic response prescriptions can disagree with measurements and thermodynamic expectations in different ways; patch potentials and geometry add complications.
why: Clarifies equilibrium fluctuations and improves precision-force interpretation.
key_works: Klimchitskaya, Mohideen, and Mostepanenko, 2009, *The Casimir Force between Real Materials: Experiment and Theory*, arXiv:0902.4022.

title: Attainable limits of near-field radiative heat transfer
open: Determine and approach practical bounds on broadband near-field heat transfer under realistic material dispersion, nonlocality, finite size, and minimum-gap constraints.
status: Large enhancements beyond far-field radiation are demonstrated; idealized bounds are not automatically achievable devices.
why: Enables thermal control and energy conversion at nanoscale separations.
key_works: Polder and van Hove, 1971, *Theory of Radiative Heat Transfer between Closely Spaced Bodies*; Miller, Johnson, and Rodriguez, 2015, *Shape-Independent Limits to Near-Field Radiative Heat Transfer*.

title: Warm-dense-matter equation of state
subfield: Chemical physics, thermal physics, and extreme materials
open: Predict and measure thermodynamic and transport properties where strong coupling, partial ionization, and quantum degeneracy coexist, with independently validated uncertainties.
status: First-principles simulations and dynamic-compression experiments constrain selected materials and paths, but broad predictive coverage remains incomplete.
why: Supports planetary science, high-energy-density experiments, and fusion modeling.
key_works: Graziani et al., editors, 2014, *Frontiers and Challenges in Warm Dense Matter*; Wadas et al., 2026, *Shock Compression of Liquid Helium to 360 GPa*, DOI: 10.1103/87r3-tgy1.

title: Solid metallic hydrogen and its retained phases
subfield: Chemical physics, thermal physics, and extreme materials
open: Establish the structures, electronic properties, and reproducibility of metallic solid hydrogen, including whether any useful phase can persist after pressure reduction.
status: Conducting dense hydrogen and debated solid-state claims do not settle the complete structural and metastability questions.
why: Tests extreme quantum matter and potential high-energy-density materials.
key_works: Wigner and Huntington, 1935, *On the Possibility of a Metallic Modification of Hydrogen*; McMahon et al., 2012, *The Properties of Hydrogen and Helium under Extreme Conditions*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.84.1607.

title: Experimental liquid–liquid critical point of water
subfield: Chemical physics, thermal physics, and extreme materials
open: Establish or exclude a liquid–liquid critical point in real water through measurements that distinguish liquid behavior from crystallization and model-dependent inference.
status: Simulations support liquid–liquid transitions in several models. The 2026 “direct observation” study cited here concerns simulation, not direct observation in a macroscopic water experiment.
why: Could unify many anomalies of supercooled water.
key_works: Poole et al., 1992, *Phase Behaviour of Metastable Water*; Wang, Berrens, and Donadio, 2026, *Direct Observation of Liquid–Liquid Phase Coexistence in Deeply Supercooled Water Using an Accurate Polarizable Multipole Model*, DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2526573123.

title: Predictive heterogeneous ice nucleation
subfield: Chemical physics, thermal physics, and extreme materials
open: Predict nucleation rates and pathways on chemically and structurally realistic surfaces without fitting each substrate separately.
status: Atomistic studies reveal mechanisms, but rare events, surface disorder, and strong temperature dependence impede quantitative transfer.
why: Improves cloud physics, cryopreservation, and icing control.
key_works: Sanz et al., 2013, *Homogeneous Ice Nucleation at Moderate Supercooling from Molecular Simulation*; Sosso et al., 2016, *Crystal Nucleation in Liquids: Open Questions and Future Challenges in Molecular Dynamics Simulations*, arXiv:1603.044 nucleation identifier (verify).

title: Predictive thermal boundary conductance
subfield: Chemical physics, thermal physics, and extreme materials
open: Calculate interface heat conductance from atomic structure, bonding, disorder, and temperature with accuracy transferable across dissimilar materials.
status: Acoustic and diffuse-mismatch models capture limits; real interfaces require anharmonic, electronic, and structural effects.
why: Removes a major bottleneck in electronics and thermal-management design.
key_works: Swartz and Pohl, 1989, *Thermal Boundary Resistance*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.61.605; Chen et al., 2022, *Interfacial Thermal Resistance: Past, Present, and Future*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.94.025002.

title: Microscopic identity of amorphous two-level systems
subfield: Chemical physics, thermal physics, and extreme materials
open: Identify the atomic structures and dynamics responsible for low-temperature two-level-system behavior in relevant amorphous materials and predict their density and coupling.
status: Phenomenological tunneling models date to the 1970s; a universal microscopic account remains elusive.
why: Reduces loss and noise in superconducting circuits, resonators, and precision sensors.
key_works: Anderson, Halperin, and Varma, 1972, *Anomalous Low-Temperature Thermal Properties of Glasses and Spin Glasses*; Phillips, 1972, *Tunneling States in Amorphous Solids*.

title: Controlled nonadiabatic molecular dynamics
subfield: Chemical physics, thermal physics, and extreme materials
open: Predict coupled electronic–nuclear dynamics through conical intersections and charge-transfer events with reliable error estimates for chemically realistic systems.
status: Surface hopping, Ehrenfest dynamics, and wavepacket methods each have important strengths and limitations; no single affordable method is uniformly reliable.
why: Enables predictive photochemistry, catalysis, and radiation-damage modeling.
key_works: John Tully, 1990, *Molecular Dynamics with Electronic Transitions*; Subotnik et al., 2016, *Understanding the Surface Hopping View of Electronic Transitions and Decoherence*.

title: First-principles electrochemical double layer
subfield: Chemical physics, thermal physics, and extreme materials
open: Predict interfacial structure, capacitance, and reaction energetics at controlled electrode potential for realistic electrolytes, including fluctuations and specific adsorption.
status: Continuum and atomistic approaches each capture parts; constant-potential sampling and long timescales remain challenging.
why: Improves batteries, electrocatalysis, and electrochemical manufacturing.
key_works: Schmickler and Santos, 2010, *Interfacial Electrochemistry*; Schwarz and Sundararaman, 2020, *The Electrochemical Interface in First-Principles Calculations*.

title: Protein-folding kinetics from sequence
open: Predict folding pathways, intermediate populations, and rate constants from sequence and environment, not merely the final structure.
status: Accurate structure prediction does not solve folding dynamics. Simulations reach useful regimes but remain limited by timescales and force-field errors.
why: Explains misfolding, kinetic traps, and functional conformational changes.
key_works: Dill and MacCallum, 2012, *The Protein-Folding Problem, 50 Years On*; Outeiral, Nissley, and Deane, 2022, *Current Structure Predictors Are Not Learning the Physics of Protein Folding*.

title: Intrinsically disordered protein ensembles in cells
open: Predict condition-dependent conformational ensembles and interaction kinetics of disordered proteins inside crowded, chemically heterogeneous living environments.
status: In vitro measurements and simulations constrain ensembles, but transferring them into cells remains difficult.
why: Links sequence to regulation and disease where a single structure is inadequate.
key_works: van der Lee et al., 2014, *Classification of Intrinsically Disordered Regions and Proteins*; Das and Pappu, 2013, *Conformations of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins Are Influenced by Linear Sequence Distributions of Oppositely Charged Residues*.

title: Causal function of biomolecular condensates
open: Determine when phase separation itself causes a cellular function, rather than merely accompanying changes in concentration, binding, or molecular organization.
status: Many condensates and mechanisms are characterized; separating phase behavior from correlated biochemical effects remains a major experimental challenge.
why: Makes condensate-targeting interventions mechanistically meaningful.
key_works: Banani et al., 2017, *Biomolecular Condensates: Organizers of Cellular Biochemistry*, DOI: 10.1038/nrm.2017.7; Hyman et al., 2014, *Liquid–Liquid Phase Separation in Biology*.

title: Predictive chromosome dynamics
open: Predict time-dependent chromatin organization and its response to molecular perturbations, linking polymer mechanics, loop extrusion, transcription, and nuclear constraints.
status: Contact maps and polymer models explain many structures, but static agreement does not uniquely identify dynamics or causal mechanisms.
why: Connects genome organization to regulation and mechanical integrity.
key_works: Dekker and Mirny, 2016, *The 3D Genome as Moderator of Chromosomal Communication*; Fudenberg et al., 2016, *Formation of Chromosomal Domains by Loop Extrusion*.

title: Tissue jamming and unjamming mechanism
open: Determine when tissue fluidization is controlled by cell shape, adhesion, propulsion, division, or extracellular matrix, and predict transitions across tissues.
status: Vertex and active-matter models reproduce important trends; universal transfer between experimental systems remains incomplete.
why: Explains collective migration, development, and invasion.
key_works: Bi et al., 2015, *A Density-Independent Rigidity Transition in Biological Tissues*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3471; Marchetti et al., 2013, arXiv:1207.2929.

title: Predictive branching morphogenesis
open: Predict organ-specific branching patterns and their robustness from local growth, mechanics, signaling, and resource constraints.
status: Models capture selected branching statistics and geometries; full parameter-to-form prediction across organs remains unfinished.
why: Supports developmental biology and tissue engineering.
key_works: Hannezo et al., 2017, *A Unifying Theory of Branching Morphogenesis*; Nerger et al., 2021, *Local Accumulation of Extracellular Matrix Regulates Global…* (full title verify), PMCID: PMC8119325.

title: Functional significance of neural criticality
open: Determine whether observed scale-free neural activity reflects genuine critical dynamics and whether proximity to criticality causally improves computation or behavior.
status: Avalanche statistics motivate criticality models, but subsampling, nonstationarity, and alternative mechanisms can generate similar signatures.
why: Tests a proposed organizing principle of brain dynamics.
key_works: Beggs and Plenz, 2003, *Neuronal Avalanches in Neocortical Circuits*; Wilting and Priesemann, 2019, *25 Years of Criticality in Neuroscience—Established Results, Open Controversies, Novel Concepts*.

title: In vivo radical-pair magnetoreception
open: Establish the complete molecular-to-neural chain by which a radical-pair reaction detects geomagnetic fields in an organism, including decisive perturbation tests.
status: Molecular experiments and behavioral effects support aspects of the mechanism; identifying the full in vivo sensor and transduction pathway remains incomplete.
why: Establishes a concrete quantum mechanism in biological sensing.
key_works: Hore and Mouritsen, 2016, *The Radical-Pair Mechanism of Magnetoreception*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-biophys-032116-094545; Luo et al., 2024, radiofrequency-orientation test, DOI: 10.1098/rsif.2024.0133.

title: Earth’s core energy budget and dynamo history
open: Reconstruct the heat and compositional power available to the geodynamo through geological time while satisfying paleomagnetic, thermal, and material constraints.
status: Core conductivity and inner-core age estimates substantially affect available power; competing histories remain possible.
why: Explains Earth’s long-lived magnetic protection and thermal evolution.
key_works: Nimmo, 2015, *Energetics of the Core*; National Academies, 2020, *A Vision for NSF Earth Sciences 2020–2030*.

title: Inner-core nucleation paradox
open: Explain how Earth’s solid inner core nucleated without requiring implausibly large supercooling, using a mechanism consistent with composition and thermal history.
status: The paradox has been sharpened by atomistic simulations. Two-step and heterogeneous mechanisms provide candidates, not a uniquely demonstrated history.
why: Determines the onset of inner-core growth and its dynamo contribution.
key_works: Huguet et al., 2018, *Earth’s Inner Core Nucleation Paradox*; Sun et al., 2022, *Two-Step Nucleation of the Earth’s Inner Core*, DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2113059119.

title: Mantle rheology across geological timescales
open: Derive constitutive laws connecting mineral defects, grain size, water content, stress, and phase changes to mantle flow over laboratory-to-geological scale gaps.
status: Laboratory creep experiments and geophysical inversions constrain different regimes; extrapolation remains a major uncertainty.
why: Improves models of convection, rebound, and tectonic evolution.
key_works: Karato, 2008, *Deformation of Earth Materials*; National Academies, 2020, *A Vision for NSF Earth Sciences 2020–2030*.

title: Initiation and persistence of plate tectonics
open: Determine the physical conditions under which a planetary lithosphere develops self-sustaining mobile plates rather than stagnant-lid or episodic behavior.
status: Numerical models demonstrate candidate mechanisms, but Earth’s onset history and the role of water and weakening remain disputed.
why: Explains planetary diversity and long-term habitability.
key_works: Bercovici and Ricard, 2014, *Plate Tectonics, Damage and Inheritance*; Korenaga, 2013, *Initiation and Evolution of Plate Tectonics on Earth: Theories and Observations*.

title: Earthquake nucleation under natural fault conditions
open: Determine which measurable fault-zone variables govern the transition from slow slip to dynamic rupture in realistic heterogeneous, fluid-bearing faults.
status: Laboratory friction laws and geophysical observations constrain mechanisms, but natural nucleation zones are poorly observed.
why: Improves physically based earthquake hazard models.
key_works: Dieterich, 1979, *Modeling of Rock Friction: 1. Experimental Results and Constitutive Equations*; Scholz, 2019, *The Mechanics of Earthquakes and Faulting*, third edition.

title: Limits of earthquake predictability
open: Determine which aspects of earthquake occurrence are predictably encoded in accessible observations, and establish calibrated gains over baseline probabilistic forecasts.
status: Reliable deterministic short-term prediction is not established. The open target includes quantitative limits, not a promise that every earthquake has a detectable precursor.
why: Separates achievable forecasting improvements from unsupported prediction claims.
key_works: Geller et al., 1997, *Earthquakes Cannot Be Predicted*; Jordan et al., 2011, *Operational Earthquake Forecasting: State of Knowledge and Guidelines for Utilization*.

title: Hydrogen–helium demixing in giant planets
open: Determine the phase-separation boundary and associated transport under giant-planet conditions, then reconcile it with luminosity and composition profiles.
status: High-pressure calculations and experiments constrain portions of the phase diagram; planetary extrapolation remains uncertain.
why: Explains helium rain and giant-planet thermal evolution.
key_works: Morales et al., 2009, *Phase Separation in Hydrogen–Helium Mixtures at Mbar Pressures*; McMahon et al., 2012, *The Properties of Hydrogen and Helium under Extreme Conditions*.

title: Ice-giant dynamo composition and geometry
open: Determine which interior phases and flow geometries produce the unusual magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune while matching gravity and thermal constraints.
status: Thin-shell and compositionally stratified dynamo models offer explanations; interior structure is weakly constrained.
why: Connects exotic high-pressure matter to planetary magnetic behavior.
key_works: Stanley and Bloxham, 2004, *Convective-Region Geometry as the Cause of Uranus’ and Neptune’s Unusual Magnetic Fields*; Redmer et al., 2011, *The Phase Diagram of Water and the Magnetic Fields of Uranus and Neptune*.

title: Low-cloud feedback
open: Quantify how low clouds respond to warming and circulation changes, including interactions among turbulence, entrainment, aerosols, and precipitation.
status: Observational constraints have improved, but cloud feedback remains a major contributor to climate-response uncertainty.
why: Narrows uncertainty in future warming.
key_works: Bony et al., 2015, *Clouds, Circulation and Climate Sensitivity*, DOI: 10.1038/ngeo2398.

title: Aerosol–cloud effective radiative forcing
open: Determine the net climate forcing from aerosol–cloud interactions with observationally constrained causal effects rather than correlations alone.
status: Aerosol properties, cloud adjustments, and meteorological confounding leave substantial uncertainty despite improving satellite and process observations.
why: Improves attribution of past warming and prediction of responses to pollution changes.
key_works: Li et al., 2026, *Advancing the Quantification of Aerosol–Cloud Interactions with…* (full title verify), DOI: 10.5194/acp-26-7705-2026; *Remaining Aerosol Forcing Uncertainty after Observational…*, 2026 (authors and full title verify).

title: Convective self-aggregation and organization
open: Predict when convection organizes into clusters, lines, or larger systems, and quantify its effects on humidity, rainfall extremes, and radiation.
status: Idealized simulations reveal several feedbacks; their importance in realistic rotating, heterogeneous atmospheres remains unsettled.
why: Improves weather extremes and climate projections.
key_works: Wing et al., 2017, *Convective Self-Aggregation in Numerical Simulations: A Review*; Bony et al., 2015, *Clouds, Circulation and Climate Sensitivity*.

title: Ocean mixing closure
open: Predict irreversible mixing from internal waves, shear instabilities, convection, and boundary processes without assuming a universal mixing efficiency.
status: Dissipation-based estimates and regional measurements are useful, but efficiency and spatial intermittency vary substantially.
why: Controls ocean heat uptake, nutrient transport, and overturning circulation.
key_works: Osborn, 1980, *Estimates of the Local Rate of Vertical Diffusion from Dissipation Measurements*; Gregg et al., 2018, *Mixing Efficiency in the Ocean*.

title: Atlantic overturning stability threshold
open: Determine the stability boundaries, recovery behavior, and observable warning indicators of Atlantic overturning under realistic forcing and freshwater perturbations.
status: Models exhibit differing sensitivities and thresholds. A precise collapse date is not established by identifying a statistical warning signal.
why: Constrains a major source of regional climate risk.
key_works: Stommel, 1961, *Thermohaline Convection with Two Stable Regimes of Flow*; IPCC, 2021, *Ocean, Cryosphere and Sea Level Change*.

title: Marine ice-sheet retreat and fracture
open: Predict grounding-line retreat, buttressing loss, hydrofracture, and possible cliff failure with constitutive laws validated across relevant scales.
status: Different model treatments produce materially different high-end sea-level outcomes; observational constraints on some failure mechanisms are sparse.
why: Reduces uncertainty in long-term sea-level rise.
key_works: Schoof, 2007, *Ice Sheet Grounding Line Dynamics: Steady States, Stability, and Hysteresis*; IPCC, 2021, *Ocean, Cryosphere and Sea Level Change*.

title: Lightning initiation
open: Explain how measured thundercloud conditions initiate leaders and breakdown, resolving the gap between observed large-scale fields and simple conventional-breakdown thresholds.
status: Streamer, hydrometeor-enhancement, and runaway-electron mechanisms provide candidate ingredients; their respective roles remain debated.
why: Explains a basic atmospheric electrical process and improves protection models.
key_works: Dwyer and Uman, 2014, *The Physics of Lightning*, DOI: 10.1016/j.physrep.2013.09.004.

title: Gravity-wave drag parameterization
open: Predict unresolved atmospheric gravity-wave generation, propagation, breaking, and momentum deposition across weather and climate models.
status: Parameterizations reproduce aspects of circulation but rely on uncertain source spectra and breaking assumptions.
why: Improves middle-atmosphere circulation and its coupling to weather.
key_works: Fritts and Alexander, 2003, *Gravity Wave Dynamics and Effects in the Middle Atmosphere*; Alexander et al., 2010, *Recent Developments in Gravity-Wave Effects in Climate Models and the Global Distribution of Gravity-Wave Momentum Flux*.

title: Attainable broadband sound-absorption limits
open: Determine and approach the best absorption achievable under simultaneous thickness, bandwidth, angle, mass, and passive-material constraints.
status: Causal bounds and highly effective prototypes exist, but jointly optimal, manufacturable designs remain unresolved for many constraint sets.
why: Enables thinner, lighter, more effective noise control.
key_works: Yang et al., 2017, *Optimal Sound-Absorbing Structures*; Dong et al., 2023, *Underwater Acoustic Metamaterials*, DOI: 10.1093/nsr/nwac246.

title: Robust broadband underwater acoustic cloaking
open: Reduce scattering over a specified bandwidth and angular range while maintaining performance under realistic pressure, structural loading, manufacturing errors, and changing environments.
status: Cloaking demonstrations commonly trade bandwidth, angle, size, or robustness. Perfect passive cloaking at all frequencies is not the proposed target.
why: Advances wave-control methods and low-scattering structures.
key_works: Cummer and Schurig, 2007, *One Path to Acoustic Cloaking*; Dong et al., 2023, *Underwater Acoustic Metamaterials*.

title: Low-loss nonreciprocal acoustic devices
open: Build useful acoustic isolators with simultaneously low insertion loss, broad bandwidth, high isolation, and stable operation at application-relevant amplitudes.
status: Nonlinear, time-modulated, and actively biased implementations break reciprocity under different assumptions; practical tradeoffs remain substantial.
why: Protects acoustic systems from reflections and enables directional signal processing.
key_works: Fleury et al., 2014, *Sound Isolation and Giant Linear Nonreciprocity in a Compact Acoustic Circulator*; Coulais et al., 2017, *Static Non-Reciprocity in Mechanical Metamaterials*.

title: Nonlinear topological mechanical-wave protection
open: Determine which topological transport protections survive finite amplitude, strong disorder, damping, and mode coupling in mechanical systems.
status: Linearized band descriptions are well developed; nonlinear operation can invalidate their assumptions.
why: Makes topological waveguiding useful beyond small laboratory signals.
key_works: Kane and Lubensky, 2014, *Topological Boundary Modes in Isostatic Lattices*; Jiao et al., 2023, *Mechanical Metamaterials and Beyond*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-023-41679-8.

title: Reliable mechanical computation
open: Demonstrate reusable mechanical logic or memory with quantified error rates, fan-out, reset cost, endurance, and environmental robustness.
status: Mechanical gates and memory elements exist; scaling them into reliable computing systems remains a separate problem.
why: Enables computation in environments unsuitable for conventional electronics.
key_works: Florijn, Coulais, and van Hecke, 2014, *Programmable Mechanical Metamaterials*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.113.175503; Jiao et al., 2023, *Mechanical Metamaterials and Beyond*.

title: Predictive fatigue lifetime from microstructure
open: Predict the distribution of failure times under realistic variable-amplitude loading from microstructure, defects, environment, and crack evolution.
status: Empirical fatigue curves are useful but transfer poorly across manufacturing routes and loading histories.
why: Improves safety and reduces overdesign.
key_works: Suresh, 1998, *Fatigue of Materials*, second edition; Ritchie, 1999, *Mechanisms of Fatigue-Crack Propagation in Ductile and Brittle Solids*.

title: Quantitative dynamic fracture branching
open: Predict when and how rapidly moving cracks branch, roughen, or change mode in three-dimensional heterogeneous materials.
status: Fracture mechanics describes many regimes, but process-zone physics and three-dimensional instabilities remain difficult to close.
why: Explains rapid catastrophic failure.
key_works: Fineberg and Marder, 1999, *Instability in Dynamic Fracture*; Bouchbinder, Fineberg, and Marder, 2010, *Dynamics of Simple Cracks*.

title: Damage-tolerant inverse-designed metamaterials
open: Design architectures whose desired mechanical response survives realistic defects, aging, and repeated loading, with experimentally validated uncertainty rather than ideal-cell simulations alone.
status: Inverse design produces remarkable nominal responses; defect tolerance and lifetime are less mature.
why: Moves architected materials from demonstrations into dependable structures.
key_works: Bertoldi et al., 2017, *Flexible Mechanical Metamaterials*; Jiao et al., 2023, *Mechanical Metamaterials and Beyond*.

title: Collider-grade muon cooling
open: Demonstrate the integrated six-dimensional phase-space cooling, transmission, and timing needed for a useful high-energy muon collider before excessive muon decay.
status: Ionization cooling is experimentally demonstrated; collider-grade integrated performance is a much stronger requirement.
why: Could enable compact access to very high lepton-collision energies.
key_works: MICE Collaboration, 2020, *Demonstration of Cooling by the Muon Ionization Cooling Experiment*; International Muon Collider Collaboration, 2024, *Interim Report*, arXiv:2407.12450.

title: High-efficiency multistage plasma acceleration
open: Preserve beam quality while coupling many plasma-acceleration stages at high repetition rate and high wall-plug efficiency.
status: High gradients and selected staging demonstrations are established; collider-quality integrated operation remains unresolved.
why: Could reduce accelerator size and cost.
key_works: Geddes, Hogan, Musumeci, and Assmann, 2022, *Report of Snowmass 21 Accelerator Frontier Topical Group 6 on Advanced Accelerators*, arXiv:2208.13279.

title: Collider-quality positron plasma acceleration
open: Accelerate positron beams with the emittance, energy spread, charge, and efficiency needed for a collider, not merely demonstrate energy gain.
status: Plasma structures naturally favorable to electrons do not automatically provide equivalent positron performance.
why: Determines whether plasma acceleration can support electron–positron colliders.
key_works: Corde et al., 2015, *Multi-Gigaelectronvolt Acceleration of Positrons in a Self-Loaded Plasma Wakefield*; Geddes et al., 2022, arXiv:2208.13279.

title: Affordable high-field accelerator dipoles
open: Manufacture long, reproducible, high-field accelerator magnets with acceptable quench protection, field quality, conductor cost, training, and lifetime.
status: Short-model records do not establish economical production of complete magnet strings.
why: Determines feasible collider energy, footprint, and cost.
key_works: Bottura et al., 2012, *Advanced Accelerator Magnets for Upgrading the LHC*; International Muon Collider Collaboration, 2024, *Interim Report*, arXiv:2407.12450.

title: Radiation-hard picosecond four-dimensional tracking
open: Combine fine spatial resolution and picosecond-class timing with low mass, manageable power, high rate, and survival of the intended radiation dose.
status: Timing sensors demonstrate important capabilities, but simultaneously meeting all next-generation detector requirements is difficult.
why: Separates overlapping collisions and expands rare-event sensitivity.
key_works: Barbeau et al., 2022, *Report of the Instrumentation Frontier Working Group for Snowmass 2021*.

title: Low-loss gravitational-wave mirror coatings
open: Produce optical coatings combining low mechanical loss, low absorption, high reflectivity, low scatter, and manufacturability at the intended temperature and wavelength.
status: Improving one property often degrades another; coating thermal noise limits important detector bands.
why: Increases gravitational-wave observatory sensitivity without simply increasing laser power.
key_works: Harry et al., 2002, *Thermal Noise in Interferometric Gravitational Wave Detectors Due to Dielectric Optical Coatings*; Granata et al., 2020, *Amorphous Optical Coatings of Present Gravitational-Wave Interferometers*.

title: Newtonian-noise cancellation for ground-based observatories
open: Predict and subtract gravity fluctuations from moving ground and air well enough to reach intended low-frequency sensitivity without subtracting genuine signals.
status: Sensor-array methods and site models provide partial demonstrations; realistic environmental variability complicates full cancellation.
why: Opens lower-frequency gravitational-wave observations from Earth.
key_works: Jan Harms, 2015, *Terrestrial Gravity Fluctuations*, arXiv:1507.05850.

title: Tenfold lower-cost cryogenic detector readout
open: As a proposed benchmark, reduce total cost and wall-plug power per usable cryogenic readout channel by tenfold against a declared reference system, holding noise, bandwidth, crosstalk, and reliability fixed.
status: Multiplexing improves selected metrics, but channel count alone does not demonstrate the complete target.
why: Makes very large quantum-sensor and detector arrays practical.
key_works: Irwin and Hilton, 2005, *Transition-Edge Sensors*; Barbeau et al., 2022, *Report of the Instrumentation Frontier Working Group for Snowmass 2021*.

title: Executable preservation of experimental analyses
subfield: Open data, benchmarks, funding, and scientific operations
open: Preserve data, calibrations, software, conditions, and expertise so an independent authorized researcher can rerun a published analysis years after the original computing environment disappears.
status: DPHEP and experiment-specific programs demonstrate feasibility; coverage and long-term operational support remain uneven.
why: Prevents expensive, irreproducible scientific data loss.
key_works: Basaglia et al., 2023, *Data Preservation in High Energy Physics*, arXiv:2302.03583.

title: Reusable public likelihoods and nuisance correlations
subfield: Open data, benchmarks, funding, and scientific operations
open: Publish enough structured likelihood information, response functions, and nuisance correlations to enable valid combinations and reinterpretations without reconstructing hidden assumptions from plots.
status: Important tools and releases exist, but practice is not universal and some analyses are difficult to release faithfully.
why: Extracts additional science without repeating experiments.
key_works: Cranmer et al., 2022, *Publishing Statistical Models: Getting the Most out of Particle Physics Experiments*, arXiv:2109.04981; Basaglia et al., 2023, arXiv:2302.03583.

title: Out-of-distribution benchmark for scientific simulators
subfield: Open data, benchmarks, funding, and scientific operations
open: Create a benchmark that tests physical accuracy, conservation, uncertainty calibration, and failure detection when learned simulators encounter new geometries, scales, materials, or forcing.
status: Existing datasets benchmark pieces of this problem; a high score on interpolation is not evidence of reliable physical extrapolation.
why: Prevents accelerated simulation from silently producing scientifically wrong results.
key_works: Shanahan et al., 2022, *Snowmass 2021 Computational Frontier CompF03 Topical Group Report: Machine Learning*, arXiv:2209.07559.

title: Cross-platform low-energy-background benchmark
subfield: Open data, benchmarks, funding, and scientific operations
open: Assemble calibrated, provenance-rich measurements of unexplained low-energy events across detector materials and laboratories, with shared environmental and analysis metadata.
status: Individual experiments publish valuable studies, but cross-platform comparability is limited; the target is harmonization, not the claim that no data exist.
why: Distinguishes new physical signals from shared material or instrumental backgrounds.
key_works: Boveia et al., 2022, *Snowmass 2021 Dark Matter Complementarity Report*, arXiv:2211.07027; Barbeau et al., 2022, instrumentation report.

title: Sustainable helium access and recovery
subfield: Open data, benchmarks, funding, and scientific operations
open: Establish procurement and recovery systems that keep helium-dependent research reliably supplied at predictable costs, including access for smaller laboratories.
status: The APS–ACS–MRS report documented serious disruption and proposed collective purchasing and recovery. The open target is durable implementation and equitable coverage, not another diagnosis.
why: Prevents cryogenic research programs from being determined by supply shocks rather than scientific merit.
key_works: APS, ACS, and MRS, 2016, *Responding to the U.S. Research Community’s Liquid Helium Crisis*.

title: Stable careers and funding for research software maintenance
subfield: Open data, benchmarks, funding, and scientific operations
open: Create and evaluate funding structures that support long-term maintenance, testing, security, and succession for critical physics software rather than rewarding only new-code creation.
status: Community roadmaps repeatedly identify maintenance and staffing needs. The gap is institutional implementation with measurable continuity, not a missing programming technique.
why: Reduces scientific risk from abandoned or undermaintained computational infrastructure.
key_works: HEP Software Foundation, 2017/2019, *A Roadmap for HEP Software and Computing R&D for the 2020s*, arXiv:1712.06982.

title: Fusion-relevant shared irradiation qualification
subfield: Open data, benchmarks, funding, and scientific operations
open: Provide accessible, adequately funded irradiation and post-irradiation facilities that produce material-qualification evidence at relevant spectra, doses, and temperatures.
status: Surrogate irradiation supplies useful information, but facility access and representative exposure remain infrastructure bottlenecks.
why: Prevents reactor design from relying on unvalidated material-lifetime assumptions.
key_works: National Academies, 2021, *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI: 10.17226/25991; Zinkle and Snead, 2014, *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*.

title: Laboratory-data funding across disciplinary boundaries
subfield: Open data, benchmarks, funding, and scientific operations
open: Establish accountable funding routes for measurements needed by another field—for example, atomic, molecular, and plasma data essential to interpreting astronomical observations.
status: National Academies assessments identify gaps when facilities, investigators, and scientific beneficiaries fall under different program responsibilities.
why: Prevents major observing facilities from being limited by comparatively inexpensive missing reference measurements.
key_works: National Academies, 2020, *Progress toward Implementation of the 2013 Decadal Survey for Solar and Space Physics: A Midterm Assessment*, discussion of laboratory-data support.

title: Theory of everything
open: Is there a singular, all-encompassing, coherent theoretical framework of physics that fully explains and links together all physical aspects of the [[universe]]?"The Unknown Universe: The Origin of the Universe, Quantum Gravity, Wormholes, and Other Things Science Still Can't Explain." Proceedings of the Royal Society of London, Series A, 1 May 2008
key_works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20physics

title: Dimensionless physical constant
open: s: At the present time, the values of various dimensionless [[physical constant]]s cannot be calculated; they can be determined only by physical measurement. What is the minimum number of dimensionless physical constants from which all other dimensionless physical constants can be derived? Are dimensional physical constants necessary at all?Alcohol constrains physical constant in the early universe." Science, 13 December 2012
key_works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20physics

title: Quantum gravity
open: Can [[quantum mechanics]] and [[general relativity]] be realized as a fully consistent theory (perhaps as a [[quantum field theory]])? Is spacetime fundamentally continuous or discrete? Would a consistent theory involve a force mediated by a hypothetical [[graviton]], or be a product of a discrete structure of spacetime itself (as in [[loop quantum gravity]])? Are there deviations from the predictions of general relativity at very small or very large scales or in other extreme circumstances that flow from a quantum gravity mechanism?
key_works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20physics

title: Black hole
open: s, [[black hole information paradox]], and [[black hole radiation]]: Do black holes produce thermal radiation, as expected on theoretical grounds? Does this radiation contain information about their inner structure, as suggested by [[gauge–gravity duality]], or not, as implied by [[Hawking radiation|Hawking]]'s original calculation? If not, and black holes can evaporate away, what happens to the information stored in them (since quantum mechanics does not provide for the destruction of information)? Or does the radiation stop at some point, leaving black hole remnants? Is there another way to probe their internal structure somehow, if such a structure [[No hair theorem|even exists]]?
key_works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20physics

title: Holographic principle
open: Is it true that [[quantum gravity]] admits a lower-dimensional description that does not contain gravity? A well-understood example of holography is the [[AdS/CFT correspondence]] in [[string theory]]. Similarly, can quantum gravity in a [[de Sitter space]] be understood using [[dS/CFT correspondence]]? Can the AdS/CFT correspondence be vastly generalized to the gauge–gravity duality for arbitrary asymptotic spacetime backgrounds? Are there other theories of quantum gravity other than string theory that admit a holographic description?
key_works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20physics

title: Quantum spacetime
open: or the emergence of spacetime: Is the nature of spacetime at the [[Planck units#Planck scale|Planck scale]] very different from the [[Spacetime#Introduction to curved spacetime|continuous classical dynamical spacetime]] that exists in general relativity? In loop quantum gravity, the spacetime is postulated to be discrete from the beginning. In string theory, although originally spacetime was considered just like in general relativity (with the only difference being [[supersymmetry]]), recent research building upon the [[Ryu–Takayanagi conjecture]] has taught that spacetime in string theory is emergent by using [[quantum information]] theoretic concepts such as [[Entropy of entanglement|entanglement entropy]] in the AdS/CFT correspondence.{{cite journal
key_works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20physics

title: Yang–Mills theory
open: Given an arbitrary [[compact space|compact]] [[gauge symmetry|gauge group]], does a non-trivial quantum Yang–Mills theory with a finite [[mass gap]] exist? (This problem is also listed as one of the [[Millennium Prize Problems]] in mathematics.)
key_works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20physics

title: Quantum field theory
open: (this is a generalization of the previous problem): Is it possible to construct, in a mathematically rigorous way, a quantum field theory in 4-dimensional spacetime that includes interactions and does not resort to [[Perturbation theory (quantum mechanics)|perturbative methods]]?
key_works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20physics

title: Cosmic inflation
open: Is the theory of cosmic inflation in the very early universe correct, and, if so, what are the details of this epoch? What is the hypothetical  [[scalar field]] that gave rise to this cosmic inflation? If inflation happened at one point, is it [[chaotic inflation|self-sustaining through inflation of quantum-mechanical fluctuations]], and thus ongoing in some extremely distant place?
key_works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20physics

title: Cosmic coincidence problem
open: the energy densities of dark energy and dark matter are of the same order of magnitude in the Universe. Dark matter energy density decreased during the evolution of the universe, so it must have been very large in the past. Is there any relation between the two energy densities?
key_works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20physics

title: Horizon problem
open: Why is the distant universe so homogeneous when the [[Big Bang theory]] seems to predict larger measurable [[Anisotropy|anisotropies]] of the night sky than those observed? Cosmological [[inflation (cosmology)|inflation]] is generally accepted as the solution, but are other possible explanations such as a [[variable speed of light]] more appropriate?
key_works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20physics

title: Size of universe
open: The diameter of the [[observable universe]] is about 93 billion light-years (or equivalently a radius of about 14 Gpc), but what is the size of the whole universe? Is the universe infinite?
key_works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20physics

title: Matter–antimatter asymmetry
open: Theoretical models suggest that the early universe should have produced equal amounts of matter and antimatter. However, observations indicate no significant primordial antimatter. Understanding the mechanisms that led to this asymmetry is a major unsolved problem in physics
key_works: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List%20of%20unsolved%20problems%20in%20physics

title: Cosmological principle
open: Is the universe homogeneous and isotropic at large enough scales, as claimed by the [[cosmological principle]] and assumed by all models that use the [[Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker metric]], including the current version of the [[Lambda-CDM model|ΛCDM model]], or is the universe [[inhomogeneous cosmology|inhomogeneous]] or anisotropic? title: Photon underproduction crisis
open: (2014–2015): This problem was resolved by Khaire and Srianand. They show that a factor 2 to 5 times large metagalactic photoionization rate can be easily obtained using updated quasar and galaxy observations. Recent observations of quasars indicate that the quasar contribution to ultraviolet photons is a factor of 2 larger than previous estimates. The revised galaxy contribution is a factor of 3 larger. These together solve the crisis

title: Hipparcos anomaly
open: (1997–2012): The High Precision Parallax Collecting Satellite (Hipparcos) measured the parallax of the [[Pleiades]] and determined a [[Pleiades#Distance|distance]] of 385 light years. This was significantly different from other measurements made by means of actual to apparent brightness measurement or [[absolute magnitude]]. The anomaly was due to the use of a weighted mean when there is a correlation between distances and distance errors for stars in clusters. It is resolved by using an unweighted mean. There is no systematic bias in the Hipparcos data when it comes to star clusters

title: Faster-than-light neutrino anomaly
open: (2011–2012): In 2011, the [[OPERA experiment]] mistakenly observed [[neutrino]]s appearing to travel [[faster-than-light|faster than light]]. On 12 July 2012 OPERA updated their paper after discovering an error in their previous flight time measurement. They found agreement of neutrino speed with the speed of light

title: Pioneer anomaly
open: (1980–2012): There was a deviation in the predicted accelerations of the [[Pioneer program|Pioneer]] 10 and 11 spacecraft as they left the Solar System. It is believed that this is a result of previously unaccounted-for [[thermal recoil force]]
